title: UK Attitudes towards Germany Survey
text:
### UK Attitudes towards Germany Survey

### Executive Summary

Deltapoll’s survey of attitudes towards Germany, commissioned by the German Embassy in London, shows a positive view of the country among much of the UK population, but also a proportion of people for whom Germany holds less interest.

Germany is regarded as an important international partner of the United Kingdom. The UK population are divided over precisely how close the relationship between the UK and Germany actually is. However, nearly half of respondents describe the relationship as good; around a third say the relationship is neither good nor bad.

At the same time, a strong majority of nearly seven in ten UK adults have a positive view of Germany, with relatively little difference in numbers between different areas of the UK or different age groups. Not only do more men than women in the UK hold a positive view of Germany, men in the UK are also more likely to say they are interested in and knowledgeable about what goes on in the country. Nonetheless, only slightly more than a third of all UK adults say they are interested in what goes on day-to-day in Germany. In terms of specific interests, German culture, Germany as a travel destination for tourists and Germany's role in the world top the list of interests for the people of the UK.

Overall, a third of respondents believe that the relationship between Germany and the UK has deteriorated since Brexit; about one in seven believe the relationship has improved. When asked to consider changes to various aspects of the relationship between the UK and Germany since the Brexit referendum in 2016, pluralities say that either the relationship has stayed the same or that they don’t know. It is in the areas of general political cooperation and trade & investment where the highest net negative results occur (-11 and -13 respectively).

There is strong support for seeing the UK and Germany work more closely together in the future. The areas where UK respondents are most likely to want the UK to work more closely with Germany include trade and investment, defence and international security, taking action on climate change and environmental protection, along with energy security and the move to renewable energy. Similarly, there is strong support for the UK to work more closely with the European Union in many areas.

As part of the survey, many narratives concerning modern Germany were explored. A majority of respondents in the UK agree with statements such as ‘People living in Germany generally have a high quality of life’, ‘Germany, by its actions, is facing up to its responsibility for crimes committed during the Nazi era, including the Holocaust’ and ‘Generally speaking, Germany is a relatively equal society’. Furthermore, a plurality of UK adults agree that, ‘Nowadays Germany is the strongest economic power in Europe’, ‘Germany is a leading power in the field of environmental protection’ and ‘Nowadays Germany is the strongest political power in Europe’.

Deltapoll interviewed 2,064 UK adults online between 1st and 4th September 2023. The data have been weighted to be representative of the UK adult population as a whole.

## Results Summary

### UK partners

The United States is the country most likely to be named as a partner of the United Kingdom, chosen by almost six in ten (59%) respondents. Australia (44%) and Canada (37%) follow next, along with New Zealand (36%). Germany comes sixth on the list, selected by fewer than a quarter (23%). This places Germany second among non-English speaking countries, behind France which is on 27%.

### UK-German bilateral relations

A narrow plurality of almost half (48%) of respondents consider the relationship between the United Kingdom and Germany to be close, including one in twenty (5%) who consider it to be very close. Four in ten (40%) do not consider the relationship between the two countries to be close.

Nearly half (49%) of respondents would describe the relationship between the United Kingdom and Germany as good, including 7% who would describe it as very good. Around a third (34%) say the relationship is neither good nor bad, while one in twenty (5%) consider the two countries to have a bad relationship.

A quarter (25%) of respondents select technology and innovation as a way in which German businesses currently contribute to the UK; food supplies and energy supplies follow thereafter (23% and 21% respectively).

A very narrow plurality of 34% think the relationship between the United Kingdom and Germany has stayed the same since the Brexit vote in 2016. A similar proportion of 33% think the relationship has become worse since then, while 14% say the relationship has improved.

When asked to consider changes to various aspects of the relationship between the United Kingdom and Germany since the Brexit vote, pluralities say that either the relationship has stayed the same or that they don’t know in response to every attribute given.

More than a third (34%) think that general political cooperation between the United Kingdom and Germany has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. A quarter (25%) think it has become worse, and almost three in ten (27%) don’t know.

Regarding defence and international security, a plurality of almost four in ten (37%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. A fifth (20%) think the relationship has got better, while 15% think it has deteriorated. Again, almost three in ten (29%) don’t know.

When it comes to trade and investment, the same proportions say that the relationship has stayed the same (29%) or has got worse (29%). Around one in six (16%) say it has improved, and almost three in ten (27%) don’t know.

Regarding research and innovation, more than a third (35%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. Almost a fifth (19%) think the relationship has got better, while 14% think it has deteriorated. More than three in ten (32%) say they don’t know.

When it comes to taking action on climate change and environmental protection, a plurality of 35% think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. A fifth (21%) think the relationship has improved since then, while fewer than one in seven (13%) think it has deteriorated. Almost a third (32%) don’t know.

A plurality (34%) do not know whether the relationship has become better or worse regarding energy security and the move to renewable energy. More than three in ten (31%) consider it to have stayed the same, while similar proportions say that it has got better (17%) or got worse (18%).

A plurality (35%) don’t know how the relationship regarding exchange trips for school pupils and other young people has changed since the Brexit vote. A third (33%) say that it has stayed the same, and similar proportions say that it has got better (15%) and got worse (17%).

When it comes to teaching skills and abilities required for a particular job or career, a plurality of 34% think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. Around a sixth (17%) think the relationship has improved since then, while fewer than one in seven (13%) think it has deteriorated. More than a third (36%) don’t know.

Regarding providing study and internship opportunities in each other's countries, around a third (32%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. A fifth (20%) think the relationship has got worse in this respect, while one in six (16%) think it has improved. A third (33%) say they don’t know.

On town twinnings almost four in ten (37%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote, and the same proportion say they don’t know. Similar proportions say the relationship has got better (13%) or got worse (12%).

When it comes to cultural events and tours, a plurality (41%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. Almost one in five (18%) consider the relationship to have improved since then, whilst fewer than one in seven (12%) think it has deteriorated. Almost three in ten (29%) say they don’t know.

The picture is similar regarding sporting events and tours – 41% consider the relationship to have stayed the same since the Brexit vote, 20% think it has got

better, and 10% think it has got worse. Again, almost three in ten (28%) say they don’t know.

Regarding general tourism and visits, more than four in ten (41%) think the relationship has stayed the same since the Brexit vote. More than a fifth (22%) think the relationship has got better, while 16% think it has deteriorated. This time, 22% say they don’t know – the lowest proportion of don’t know responses of all the aspects given.

More than four in ten (42%) would like to see the United Kingdom and Germany working more closely together on trade and investment in future. Almost four in ten (36%) would like to see the two countries work more closely on defence and international security. More than a third (34%) would like to see closer cooperation on taking action on climate change and environmental protection, and the same proportion (34%) on energy security and the move to renewable energy. Nine of the areas listed had more than a fifth of respondents saying they were an area where United Kingdom and Germany should work more closely together.

### Perceptions of and interest in Germany

A strong majority of nearly seven in ten (69%) respondents hold a positive view of Germany. Around one in six (16%) say their view of Germany is negative, while a similar proportion (15%) say they do not know.

A narrow majority (51%) of respondents say they do not know much about what goes on day-to-day in Germany nowadays. Just over a fifth (21%) know either a great deal or a fair amount, while a further 22% know nothing at all.

A plurality (45%) do not know whether Germany is the strongest military power in Europe nowadays. A third (33%) disagree with the statement, whereas a fifth (21%) agree.

More than four in ten (42%) respondents agree that nowadays Germany is the strongest economic power in Europe, including almost one in ten (9%) who strongly agree. Around a quarter (24%) disagree, while more than a third (35%) don’t know.

More than a third (36%) of respondents agree that nowadays Germany is the strongest political power in Europe, while fewer than three in ten (27%) disagree. Again, a sizeable proportion of 36% say they do not know.
